analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to spend heavily on advertising and posting consumer product recalls.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from June 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force companies whose products are recalled to spend real money telling the public — at least 25% of what they spent marketing the product, plus their entire internet marketing budget, on recall advertising within a year. It would also require them to keep the recall notice on their websites until at least 95% of buyers respond, post it on their social media accounts monthly for a year, and let the Consumer Product Safety Commission order importers — not just domestic distributors — to stop selling dangerous products. It also requires the agency to publish recall participation rates so Congress and the public can see how many people actually got their money back or returned a hazard.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who own recalled products — including parents with recalled cribs, car seats, and toys — who today often never learn a product they own has been recalled. The bill's findings note 400+ products are recalled yearly and typical consumer response rates run 4–18% [S3]. CPSC gains stronger tools, since it could order importers to cease distribution and could require advertising plans before approving any recall plan [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires companies to spend on recall advertising an amount equal to at least 25% of their peak 12-month traditional marketing spend for the product, plus all of their internet marketing spend for it, within 365 days of an approved recall plan [S3].

Requires companies to post recall notices on their own websites until recall participation reaches at least 95%, and on each social media account they maintain at least 5 times a month for 12 months [S3].
Requires the CPSC to order public notice of recalls (changing 'may order' to 'shall order') and extends cease-distribution orders to importers, closing a gap for goods made overseas [S3].

Blocks settlement offers that don't commit the company to the same public-notification duties, and applies the same notice duties to voluntary corrective actions, so companies can't quietly settle their way out of advertising a recall [S3].
Requires CPSC to publish annual data on how many products were sold, how many were remedied, and how many injuries occurred after each recall began [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, distributors, importers, and retailers of consumer products, who would bear the cost of mandated recall advertising and posting; some of that cost could be passed to consumers in prices. CPSC would also take on new reporting work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumer product makers, importers, and retailers

drawbacks.text: The advertising mandate is a floor, not a ceiling, tied to the company's own past marketing spending — so a company that heavily marketed a product could owe very large recall-advertising bills even for a low-risk defect, a cost that could land in prices [S3].

Requiring website posting until 95% participation could in theory keep notices up indefinitely, since some products sit in closets for years and a 95% response rate is far above today's typical 4–18% [S3].
Small importers and retailers could face compliance costs that are proportionally heavier for them than for large firms, since the duties don't scale by company size [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety upside is real: with typical recall response rates between 4% and 18%, most owners of dangerous products never hear about the danger, and mandated advertising directly targets that failure [S3]. The main cost is compliance spending by companies, some of which may show up in prices; the design ties the obligation to a company's own marketing budget, which is a defensible proxy for how visible the product was to buyers but is blunt for low-hazard recalls. On balance the consumer benefit is large relative to a real but bounded cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Consumer Protection subcommittee on June 7, 2021, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Grace Meng introduced the bill on June 4, 2021, with introductory remarks in the Congressional Record [S5].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on June 4, 2021, and to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce on June 7, 2021 [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers, importers, and retailers of consumer products are better off, because they avoid the mandated recall-advertising and posting costs; consumers remain exposed to recalls they never hear about, with response rates still as low as 4–18% [S3][S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Product makers and retailers, avoiding recall-ad mandates

for.name: Grace Meng
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on June 4, 2021.

for.name: 8 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only support it attracted in the chamber.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chair controlled the schedule
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee and then in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded support was the Democratic sponsor and 8 Democratic cosponsors, and the bill died in committee without any recorded opposition votes [S4][S5].

industries.note: They would have had to fund recall advertising scaled to their own past marketing budgets, post notices until 95% of buyers respond, and open settlement offers to CPSC scrutiny — costs that exist precisely to reach buyers the companies' own marketing created. The bill died before any of this took effect [S3][S5].
The bill's notice and posting duties extend to distributors and retailers of recalled products, not just manufacturers, adding compliance obligations [S3].

industries.industry: Digital advertising and social media platforms
industries.note: Mandated recall advertising — including the full prior internet-marketing spend — would have routed substantial ad dollars to online channels and social platforms, though only for recalled products [S3].
